gaps.fact: Oidium and mildew as Burgundy's vineyard diseases, and the general effect of limestone soils on vine vigour: neither is taught in a Burgundy chapter or article, and no Burgundy stem asks them.

The benefits and consequences of planting density: the article gives the figure (around ten thousand vines to the hectare) but nothing explains what the density does, and the only density stem (c-rdavnsws) is a Rhône one.

The pièce of 228 litres, cold soak before fermentation and chaptalisation as Burgundy practice: the article's winemaking paragraph is the only place that ties all three to Burgundy (the pièce is also named in the Village chapter Viticulture & Winemaking, fact 6, and in the explanation of c-5vqe7u7z, which asks the feuillette); the Régionale bank asks cold soak and chaptalisation only in general terms under Winemaking Techniques (i-4929ql8d, i-525jaico), and no question asks any of the three for Burgundy.

The oak gradients the Court wants: new oak rising from village to Premier Cru to Grand Cru in Chablis, Mâcon-Villages in steel against barrel-aged Pouilly-Fuissé, and Nouveau and Villages in tank against the crus in foudre. The articles state the Pouilly-Fuissé and cru halves; the Chablis gradient is absent and no question asks any of the three.

Louis Latour, Albert Bichot and William Fèvre, on the Court's list of larger négociants (William Fèvre printed with Bouchard Père et Fils, its owner), are in no article or chapter; of the Court's domaines only Romanée-Conti, Leflaive and Drouhin are asked in a question.
General quality levels of the Burgundy vintages of the past ten years: the Codex holds no vintage notes by house rule (nothing volatile).

Classic Burgundian dishes with the wines of Burgundy (boeuf bourguignon, coq au vin, escargots, jambon persillé) and the reasoning from oak, acid and tannin: the banks pair Chablis with oysters and Époisses with marc, and no stem pairs a red Burgundy with a Burgundian dish.

Chalk, which the Court lists beside Kimmeridgian, Portlandian, marl, schist and limestone: it appears only as the article's chalkier ground around the great white villages and as a wrong option in i-p7k6ulps; no chapter or question teaches it, while the other five are taught.

notes: Mapped questions: Régionale 63 (Burgundy), Village 49 (Burgundy), 112 in all. Beyond the map, Producers & Icons asks Leflaive and Drouhin, Food & Pairing pairs Chablis and Époisses, and Terroir: Climate & Soil carries the frost and limestone stems in general terms. The Certified column is best served on the appellation ladder, the villages and their grand crus, Chablis and Beaujolais; it is thinnest on the cellar vocabulary the Court lists by name (pièce, cold soak, chaptalisation, the three oak gradients), the two vineyard diseases and the négociant roll. No factual error found: every date and count checked (33 grands crus as 24, 8 and 1; Régnié 1988; Maranges 1989; Pouilly-Fuissé Premier Cru 2020; Saint-Bris 2003; Coteaux Bourguignons 2011; Clos des Lambrays 1981) holds. One search spent, on the Mâconnais premiers crus; nothing else in the Court's Burgundy cells has moved since 8.2023.
